source_refs.note: Topic 17.10 with Example 17.6 (PDF 99-100); Fig 17.9 (a)-(d) redrawn in the rc-rl figure. The example's capacitance printed '5 F' is read as 5 uF. The check question is added.

blocks.text: A resistance R and a capacitor C are connected in series to an AC source V (Fig 17.9 a). The same current flows through both. The voltage across R is VR = Irms R, in phase with the current; the voltage across C is VC = Irms XC = Irms / (wC), lagging the current by 90 degrees. Taking the current as the reference, VR is drawn along the current line and VC at right angles to it (Fig 17.9 b). The applied voltage is the vector sum: Vrms = square root of (VR^2 + VC^2) = Irms square root of (R^2 + (1/wC)^2). So the impedance is Z = Vrms / Irms = square root of (R^2 + (1/wC)^2) (17.21).

blocks.alt: (a) A resistor R and capacitor C in series with an AC source V; current I; double arrows mark VR across R and VC across C; small sketches show VR in phase with I and VC at right angles behind I. (b) Phasors: VR = Irms R along the current I, VC = Irms XC downwards at 90 degrees, and the resultant Vrms = Irms Z at angle theta below I.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.9 (a), (b): (a) RC series circuit; (b) voltage phasors of the RC series circuit (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.9 (a), (b)).

blocks.text: This impedance diagram (Fig 17.9 c) shows R along the reference direction and XC at right angles; Z is their vector sum. The angle theta between Z and R is the phase difference between the voltage and the current: here the current leads the voltage by theta (Fig 17.9 d), where theta = tan^-1(XC/R) = tan^-1(1/(wCR)) = tan^-1(1/(2 pi f C R)).

blocks.alt: (c) Impedance diagram: R horizontal, XC downwards at right angles and Z the diagonal at angle theta to R. (d) Voltage V and current I against omega t from 0 to 360 degrees, with the same period; I reaches each point a phase angle theta before V.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.9 (c), (d): (c) Impedance diagram of RC series circuit; (d) voltage and current waveform in RC-series circuit (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.9 (c), (d)).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 17.9(d) draws voltage and current 90 degrees apart and at different frequencies. In a series RC circuit both have the same frequency and the current leads the voltage by the angle theta, as drawn above.

The power consumed in an RC series circuit is due to the resistor, because the capacitor only stores energy and does not dissipate it: P = I^2 R, or P = VI cos(theta) (17.22), where theta is the phase angle between voltage and current.

A 5 kilo-ohm resistor is connected in series with a 5 uF capacitor across a 220 V, 50 Hz AC source. Find the phase angle. Solution: theta = tan^-1(1/(2 pi f C R)) = tan^-1[1/(2 x 3.14 x 50 Hz x 5 x 10^-6 F x 5000 ohm)] = tan^-1(0.1273) = 7.25 degrees.
